subject: General Knowledge
topic: Seven Wonders of the World — mixed tiers

questions.stem: Among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, which is the only structure that survives substantially intact to the present day?

options.option_text: Statue of Zeus at Olympia, Greece
Great Pyramid of Giza, Egypt
Hanging Gardens of Babylon, Mesopotamia
Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, Turkey

questions.explanation: B is correct. The Great Pyramid of Giza (c. 2560 BC) is the sole Ancient Wonder still standing, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The other six wonders were destroyed by fire, earthquake, or gradual decay — the Temple of Artemis was burned down and later demolished, the Statue of Zeus perished in a fire, and the Hanging Gardens' very existence remains disputed by historians.

questions.stem: The New Seven Wonders of the World were announced in 2007 following a global public poll organised by the New7Wonders Foundation. Which Indian monument was selected in this list?

options.option_text: Qutub Minar, a UNESCO site in New Delhi
Taj Mahal, the white marble mausoleum in Agra, UP
Red Fort Complex, a Mughal stronghold in Delhi
Sun Temple of Konark, a UNESCO site in Odisha

questions.explanation: B is correct. The Taj Mahal was the only Indian monument chosen in the New Seven Wonders of the World 2007 poll, joining the Great Wall of China, Christ the Redeemer, Machu Picchu, Chichen Itza, the Roman Colosseum, and Petra. Qutub Minar and Konark are UNESCO sites but were not part of this selection. Red Fort, also UNESCO-listed, was never a serious finalist in that poll.

questions.stem: Dholavira, inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2021, is significant primarily as one of the largest and best-preserved urban sites belonging to which ancient civilisation?

options.option_text: Vedic Aryan culture of the Indo-Gangetic plain
Indus Valley (Harappan) Civilisation in Gujarat
Mauryan urban settlements of western India
Dravidian pre-historic Bronze Age settlements

questions.explanation: B is correct. Dholavira on Khadir Island (Rann of Kutch, Gujarat) is one of the five largest Harappan cities and unique for its sophisticated water conservation system and multi-layered defences. It was occupied c. 3000–1500 BCE. The Vedic and Mauryan civilisations are geographically and chronologically distinct from the Harappan culture; attributing Dholavira to them is the most common distractor error in exams.

questions.stem: The Rudresvara (Ramappa) Temple, accorded UNESCO World Heritage status in 2021, is renowned for its lightweight 'floating bricks' made of vesicular material. In which Indian state is it located?

options.option_text: Karnataka, known for Hoysala temple architecture
Andhra Pradesh, near the Krishna River delta zone
Telangana, in Palampet village near Warangal
Odisha, famous for its Kalinga style of architecture

questions.explanation: C is correct. The Ramappa Temple (named after its sculptor) stands at Palampet, Mulugu district, Telangana, and was built in 1213 CE under the Kakatiya ruler Ganapati Deva. The 'floating bricks' are lightweight frothy bricks that stay buoyant in water — an extraordinary medieval engineering feat. Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh are the most common wrong answers since students associate Kakatiya culture with the undivided Andhra Pradesh state.

questions.stem: Among all of India's UNESCO World Heritage Sites, which one holds the unique distinction of being classified as a 'Mixed Heritage Site' — meaning it satisfies criteria for BOTH outstanding natural AND cultural value?

options.option_text: Sundarbans National Park, West Bengal (mangrove delta)
Manas Wildlife Sanctuary, Assam (biodiversity hotspot)
Khangchendzonga National Park, Sikkim (sacred mountains)
Nanda Devi and Valley of Flowers, Uttarakhand (alpine flora)

questions.explanation: C is correct. Khangchendzonga NP (Sikkim), inscribed in 2016, is India's first and only 'mixed' UNESCO site — it meets both natural criteria (exceptional biodiversity, glaciers, high-altitude ecosystems) and cultural criteria (sacred landscapes, myths, and living traditions of the Sikkimese, Lepcha, and Limbu communities). Sundarbans, Manas, and Nanda Devi are purely natural inscriptions. This 'mixed' classification is a high-frequency exam angle.

questions.stem: Which of the following UNESCO World Heritage Sites in India is CORRECTLY matched with its year of inscription?

options.option_text: Fatehpur Sikri, Uttar Pradesh — inscribed in 1986
Mahabodhi Temple Complex, Bihar — inscribed in 2000
Red Fort Complex, Delhi — inscribed in 2009
Elephanta Caves, Maharashtra — inscribed in 1988

questions.explanation: A is correct. Fatehpur Sikri was inscribed in 1986 along with the Agra Fort. The Mahabodhi Temple Complex was inscribed in 2002, not 2000 (candidates often confuse this with the year 2000 itself). The Red Fort was inscribed in 2007, not 2009. Elephanta Caves were inscribed in 1987, not 1988 — a single-year shift that is a classic exam trap. Precise inscription-year recall is tested in RRB NTPC and SSC CGL Tier-II papers.

questions.stem: The 'Hoysala Sacred Ensembles,' India's 42nd UNESCO World Heritage Site inscribed in 2023, include the Chennakeshava Temple at Belur and Hoysaleshwara Temple at Halebidu. Which is the THIRD temple site included in this ensemble?

options.option_text: Somnathpur, featuring the Keshava (Trikuta) Temple in Karnataka
Pattadakal, seat of Chalukya coronation temples in Karnataka
Badami, site of rock-cut Chalukya cave temples in Karnataka
Aihole, known as the cradle of Indian temple architecture

questions.explanation: A is correct. The Keshava Temple at Somnathpur (Mysuru district, Karnataka), built in 1268 CE by Somanatha Dandanayaka, is the third Hoysala site in the ensemble. It is a trikuta (triple-shrined) temple famous for its intricate star-shaped platform and sculptural friezes. Pattadakal, Badami, and Aihole are all Karnataka temples but belong to the Chalukya dynasty, not Hoysala — students confuse them because all are Karnataka archaeological gems and even UNESCO-listed themselves (Pattadakal alone, since 1987).
